teaser: She is sprinting and rooted to the spot in the same instant. Bernini carved the split second between.
review_notes:
Dates: begun 1622, finished 1625, with an interruption for the David (1623 to 1624); metadata year 1625 is the completion.
The role of the assistant Giuliano Finelli in carving the leaves, roots and hair is well documented but its exact extent is debated.
The Latin couplet by Cardinal Maffeo Barberini (later Urban VIII) is paraphrased, not quoted; its cartouche on the base is not visible in this photo.
Original placement against a wall near a door, so that visitors first saw Apollo from behind: based on research on the Villa Borghese display, to verify.
The statement that restorers found the thin leaves ring when tapped is a frequently repeated report: verify or remove.
Apollo's left hand resting on bark at Daphne's waist is true of the sculpture but hidden from this camera angle, so it is only mentioned in text.
Height 2.43 m.

lesson.text: Everything about her says speed: the hair thrown upward, the arms flung out, the mouth open in a shout. And yet her feet will never move again. In this one figure, a girl is running flat out and standing as still as a tree. Both are true at once.

The story comes from the Roman poet Ovid. The god Apollo mocks Cupid, the little god of love, who takes revenge with two arrows. A golden one makes Apollo fall for the nymph Daphne. A lead one makes her want nothing to do with him. He chases. She runs until her strength gives out.

At the last moment Daphne begs her father, a river god, to destroy the beauty that caused all this. He turns her into a laurel tree. A painter could show the before or the after. Gian Lorenzo Bernini, at twenty-three, decided to carve the change itself, while it is happening.

lesson.title: A body becoming a tree
lesson.text: The change does not hit all of her at once. Travel upward, from the ground to her fingertips.

spots.title: Toes
spots.text: Her toes have just touched down, and thin roots already stretch out of them into the soil. This is where the running stops.

spots.title: Bark
spots.text: A sheet of rough bark climbs her leg and hip like a wave. Bernini textures it with tiny tool marks, so it looks dry and dull next to her polished skin.

spots.title: Hair
spots.text: Her hair flies up and back, as if she had been stopped dead. Follow the locks outward and they flatten into leaves.

spots.title: Fingers
spots.text: Each finger ends in a spray of laurel. The leaves are carved so thin that light passes through the marble.

lesson.text: Notice which parts are still human: her face, her torso, her voice. She knows what is happening to her. And the god behind her does not, not yet. His hand has reached her waist, and what it touches there is no longer skin. It is bark.

Marble this thin is terrifying to carve: one slip and a leaf snaps. Much of the foliage and the roots is credited to Giuliano Finelli, a young assistant with an astonishing touch for fine detail. He felt he never got proper credit and later left Bernini's workshop.

Stone is heavy and brittle. Marble statues before this one tend to keep their limbs close to the body, for safety. Here arms, cloth and branches shoot into empty air. Bernini makes that possible with a hidden trick of balance, and he uses the same lines to tell you who is winning the race.
Three movements run through the pair.

lines.label: The chase
lines.text: One long diagonal runs from Apollo's back foot to Daphne's raised hand. Both bodies lean along it, like a single arrow in flight.

lines.label: Her arc
lines.text: Daphne's body bows away from him, hips forward, shoulders back. The trunk rising along her leg doubles as the solid column that carries the weight of the whole group.

lines.label: The wake
lines.text: Apollo's cloth and his trailing arm stream out behind him. They are the wind of the run made visible, and they balance the mass leaning forward.

lesson.text: Bernini made marble do what it should not: show time passing. You are looking at a before, a during and an after, packed into one block.

This love of the peak moment, of drama and movement that spills into the viewer's space, is the heart of the style called Baroque, which took hold in Rome in the 1600s. Bernini was its great inventor in sculpture, and this group, finished in 1625, was his proof.

The patron was a cardinal, Scipione Borghese, and a nude pagan chase in a churchman's villa needed an excuse. Another cardinal, the future Pope Urban VIII, supplied two lines of Latin for the base. Their moral: whoever runs after fleeting pleasure ends up holding leaves and bitter berries.

Bernini also thought about where you would be standing. The group was first set near a wall, so that a visitor walking in saw Apollo from behind, mid-stride. Only by stepping around did you find Daphne, and the leaves. The statue staged its own surprise.
Even from this side, he has tucked in details that reward a slow eye. One of them sits right between the two bodies, and it is easy to take for cloth.
A leafy branch has already sprouted in the gap between Apollo and Daphne. Can you find it?

spots.title: The first branch
spots.text: A bunch of laurel leaves pushes out from the trunk at hip height, right against Apollo's fluttering cloth. The tree is growing into the space where he hoped to hold her.

lesson.text: In Ovid's poem, Apollo does not give up his prize entirely. Since Daphne cannot be his wife, he declares the laurel his tree. That is why poets, generals and athletes in the ancient world were crowned with laurel wreaths, and why the word “laureate” still means a winner.

Restorers who cleaned the group have reported that the thinnest leaves give a clear, ringing note when tapped lightly, like crystal. The statue has never left the villa it was made for, today the Galleria Borghese.
Go back to that first impression: running and rooted. Now you can place the exact point where one becomes the other, in a toe, a fingertip, a hand that expected skin.

quiz.question: Which poet tells the story of Apollo and Daphne?
quiz.explanation: The tale comes from the Roman poet Ovid.

quiz.question: What tree does Daphne become?
quiz.explanation: Her father turns her into a laurel, which Apollo then adopts as his tree.

quiz.question: How does Bernini make the bark look different from skin?
options: He left it rough with tiny tool marks while polishing the skin
quiz.explanation: The bark is textured and dull, the skin smooth and polished.

quiz.question: What does the trunk along Daphne's leg also do?
options: It hides a crack in the marble
It carries the weight of the group
quiz.explanation: The rising trunk works as the solid support for the leaning figures.

quiz.question: Who is credited with much of the delicate foliage?
quiz.explanation: Finelli carved many of the leaves and roots and felt he was not credited.

quiz.question: What was the visitor meant to see first when the group stood near a wall?
quiz.explanation: You first saw Apollo's back, then discovered the transformation by walking around.

facts.text: Bernini chose to show Daphne after she had fully become a tree.
facts.explanation: He carved the transformation in progress: roots, bark and leaves on a body still human.

facts.text: A future pope wrote a moral verse for the statue's base.
facts.explanation: Cardinal Maffeo Barberini, later Urban VIII, supplied two lines of Latin.

facts.text: Cupid shot Apollo and Daphne with the same kind of arrow.
facts.explanation: A golden arrow made Apollo fall in love, a lead one made Daphne reject him.
